definition: Input/output: any transfer of data between the CPU and memory on one side and the outside world on the other, such as disks, network cards, keyboards and screens. An operating system spends much of its design effort making I/O efficient and uniform.
example: Reading a file, receiving a network packet and noticing a key press are all I/O.

definition: A piece of hardware the computer exchanges data with, such as an SSD, a network card, a keyboard or a GPU. It is usually made of the physical mechanism plus a device controller that the CPU talks to.

Hardware that manages a device and presents a command/data interface to host software, often with firmware and its own processor. In the controller-based examples here, the driver commands the controller rather than directly driving the physical mechanism.

A small storage location inside a device controller that the CPU reads or writes to control the device. Typical registers are a status register (busy? error?), a command register (what to do) and a data register (bytes in or out).
example: A driver polls the status register until its BUSY bit clears, then writes WRITE into the command register.

definition: Software stored inside a device and run by the device's own processor, for example the code inside an SSD controller or a network card. It is separate from the operating system's driver.

Non-Volatile Memory Express: a family of interfaces and protocols for non-volatile storage. The PCIe transport uses memory-based submission/completion queues and doorbells; NVMe also has fabric transports such as TCP and RDMA.

Solid-state drive: storage using electronic memory rather than moving read/write heads, commonly NAND flash. Latency depends on device, operation and workload; there is no universal read-time guarantee.

PCI Express: the high-speed serial expansion bus, successor to the older parallel PCI bus, that connects devices such as SSDs, network cards and GPUs to the CPU. Devices on it expose their registers through BARs and can perform DMA into RAM.

A way of reaching device registers through a separate I/O address space, using special instructions (`in` and `out` on x86) rather than ordinary memory loads and stores. It is mostly a legacy mechanism today.

Memory-mapped I/O: device registers appear at certain physical memory addresses, so an ordinary load or store (with the right mapping and ordering rules) reads or writes the device instead of RAM. It is how modern drivers talk to PCIe devices.
example: Writing to the NVMe doorbell register is an MMIO store to an address inside the drive's BAR.

definition: The family of CPU instruction sets used by Intel and AMD processors in most PCs and servers. It is one of the two dominant architectures, alongside Arm.
A family of CPU instruction sets used in almost all phones and increasingly in servers and laptops (for example Apple silicon and AWS Graviton). Its interrupt controller is called the GIC.
An address as seen on the memory bus, after any virtual-memory translation. RAM and device registers each occupy ranges of the physical address space.

An address used by kernel code before CPU virtual-memory translation. In conventional mapped DMA, a device uses an address supplied by the DMA API instead; supported shared virtual addressing is a separate mechanism.

Linux MMIO helpers: ioremap creates an appropriate mapping, while readl and writel read or write a 32-bit device register through it. Drivers must follow the accessor and ordering rules for their platform.
Base address register: a PCI/PCIe configuration register that says where in the physical address space a device's registers or memory window appear. A driver maps the BAR to reach the device by MMIO.
A free, widely used operating-systems textbook by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau. Its I/O chapter supplies the canonical polling-device protocol used in this module.

Repeatedly checking whether something is ready (a status register, a ring, a socket) instead of waiting to be told. It avoids interrupt and wake-up costs but uses CPU while checking; busy-polling checks continuously.

Waiting by repeatedly checking a condition while remaining runnable, consuming CPU time instead of sleeping. Whether it is appropriate depends on expected wait duration, notification cost and available CPU budget.
I/O in which the CPU itself moves every byte between a device's data register and memory. It is simple but costs CPU time proportional to the data size; DMA replaces it for bulk transfers.

A signal from a device that makes the CPU pause what it is running, between instructions, and jump to a handler registered for that interrupt. It lets the CPU do other work instead of polling until a device finishes.
example: A disk raises an interrupt when a read completes; the handler wakes the process waiting for it.

definition: The kernel function that runs when an interrupt arrives. In Linux the hard IRQ handler (top half) runs with the current CPU's work pre-empted and cannot sleep, so it does only the minimum and defers the rest.
Interrupt request: an interrupt line or vector, or the interrupt itself. Linux numbers IRQs and shows per-CPU counts for each one in `/proc/interrupts`.

A number used to select an interrupt/exception handler entry. MSI-X permits multiple independently configured vectors; mapping a queue to a dedicated vector and CPU depends on device support, allocation and affinity.
The x86 table that maps each interrupt vector to the address of its handler. The CPU looks up this table when an interrupt or exception occurs.
Hardware that collects interrupt signals from devices and routes each one to a particular CPU. On x86 it is the APIC; on Arm it is the GIC.
Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller: the interrupt controller on x86 systems. Each CPU has a local APIC, and I/O APICs route device interrupts to them.
Generic Interrupt Controller: Arm's standard interrupt controller, which prioritises interrupts and routes them to CPU cores.

Message-signalled interrupts: a PCIe device raises an interrupt by writing a small message to a special address rather than asserting a dedicated wire. MSI-X allows up to 2,048 independent vectors per device, so a NIC can give each queue its own interrupt and CPU.
A Linux file listing every interrupt source with a count of how many times it has fired on each CPU. Useful for checking IRQ affinity and spotting interrupt storms.

Taking an interrupt for the first event, then masking it and polling while work keeps arriving, and re-enabling interrupts once the queue drains. It gets low latency when idle and low overhead when busy; Linux networking calls its version NAPI.

The Linux real-time configuration (merged into mainline in 6.12) that makes almost all kernel code pre-emptible and runs most interrupt and softirq handling in threads, changing where that work executes.

A failure under heavy network load where the CPU spends all its time handling per-packet interrupts and never runs the code that consumes the packets, so useful throughput falls as the packet rate rises. NAPI-style polling was designed to prevent it.
A device feature that raises one interrupt for a batch of events, after a count or time threshold, instead of one per event. It cuts interrupt overhead at the cost of a little added latency.

Direct memory access: a device reads or writes RAM itself, without the CPU copying each byte. The driver sets up the transfer (address, length), and the device reports completion by interrupt or a completion entry.
example: An NVMe SSD DMAs a 128 KiB read straight into the page cache, then posts a completion entry.

definition: A device that can start its own transfers on the bus, which is what lets it perform DMA into RAM without the CPU.
The address a device must use to reach a buffer by DMA. It can differ from the CPU's virtual or physical address, especially behind an IOMMU, so drivers obtain it from the DMA API.
The Linux kernel interface that drivers use to map buffers for DMA (for example `dma_map_single`), returning device-usable DMA addresses and performing any cache maintenance the platform needs.

A circular array in RAM shared by a driver and a device, each entry (descriptor) describing one buffer or command. The driver fills descriptors and rings a doorbell; the device consumes them, does the DMA and marks them complete.
A device register the driver writes (usually a new tail index) to tell the device that new entries are waiting in a descriptor ring or submission queue.
The receive (RX) and transmit (TX) descriptor rings of a network card. The NIC DMAs incoming frames into buffers listed on the RX ring and sends frames listed on the TX ring.

Keeping copies of the same memory in different caches (or seen by a device) consistent. With DMA, the CPU cache might hold stale data the device has just overwritten unless the platform or the driver keeps them coherent.
A feature on supporting devices and IOMMUs that lets a device use a process's own virtual addresses for DMA, sharing its page tables. It is separate from the conventional mapped-DMA model.
Locking memory pages in RAM so the kernel cannot move or swap them out while a device or the kernel is using them, for example during DMA into a user buffer.

Input-output memory management unit: hardware that translates and checks device DMA addresses against configured mappings. It contributes to device isolation; safe assignment also depends on hardware topology, interrupt isolation, reset behavior and configuration.
Intel VT-d and AMD-Vi are the two main IOMMU implementations on x86 systems, providing DMA remapping and interrupt remapping for device isolation.

Assigning a physical device or supported device function to a VM so its guest driver controls the device interface. Safe direct assignment normally requires suitable DMA/interrupt isolation, device groups, reset behavior and correct configuration; an IOMMU alone is not a complete guarantee.
The smallest set of devices the IOMMU can isolate from each other. VFIO assigns whole groups, because devices in one group may be able to reach each other's memory.
An IOMMU feature that checks and redirects interrupt messages from devices, so an assigned device cannot inject arbitrary interrupts into the host.
What a virtual machine believes is a physical address. The hypervisor (for the CPU) and the IOMMU (for devices) translate it to a real host physical address.
Kernel (or sometimes user-space) code that knows one kind of device controller's registers and protocol and presents it through a generic interface such as a block device, network interface or file.
A Linux device accessed through a file in `/dev` with device-specific operations such as `read`, `write` and `ioctl`, for example `/dev/null` or a serial port.
A device presented as an array of fixed-size blocks that can be read or written in any order, such as an SSD (`/dev/nvme0n1`). File systems sit on top of block devices.
In Linux, a device such as `eth0` that sends and receives packets. It has no `/dev` file and is reached through sockets and the networking stack.
The Linux directory of device files. Opening one (for example `/dev/null`, which discards writes) gives access to a character or block device through ordinary file calls.
A system call for device-specific control operations that do not fit `read` and `write`, such as setting a serial port's speed.
The Linux kernel layer between file systems and block-device drivers. It builds, merges and schedules I/O requests (the I/O scheduler decides their order) before handing them to the driver.
The fast, first part of Linux interrupt handling: the hard IRQ handler that checks and acknowledges the device, grabs anything urgent and schedules the rest.
The deferred part of Linux interrupt handling that does the slower processing after the top half returns, using a softirq, tasklet, workqueue or threaded IRQ.

Kernel execution in which sleeping is forbidden, for example conventional hard IRQ or softirq handling or code holding a non-sleeping spinlock. A task may exist, but that does not make sleeping legal in such a region.
Kernel code executing in the context of a task, such as a system call or kernel thread. It may sleep only when its current locking, preemption and interrupt rules permit it.
One of a small fixed set of Linux bottom-half handlers (networking receive and transmit, block completion, timers and a few more). They run on return from interrupts or in ksoftirqd and cannot sleep.
An older Linux bottom-half mechanism built on softirqs. Tasklets cannot sleep and are being phased out in favour of BH workqueues.
A Linux mechanism for deferring work to kernel worker threads, which run in process context and may sleep. BH workqueues are a variant that run in softirq context instead.
A workqueue created with the `WQ_BH` flag, whose items run in softirq (bottom-half) context and so cannot sleep. It is the intended replacement for tasklets.
An interrupt whose slower handling runs in a dedicated kernel thread. The top half returns `IRQ_WAKE_THREAD`, and the thread handler may then sleep. Registered with `request_threaded_irq`.

The per-CPU Linux kernel threads (ksoftirqd/0, ksoftirqd/1, ...) that run pending softirq work when there is too much to finish on interrupt return. High CPU use by one indicates heavy softirq load on that CPU.

A task used for kernel work, such as ksoftirqd or worker handling. Conventional kernel threads do not have an ordinary userspace execution context; some kernel workers temporarily borrow a user memory context, so this is not an absolute no-address-space rule.
Stopping running code before it chooses to stop, so something else can run: an interrupt pre-empts whatever was on the CPU, and the scheduler can pre-empt one thread to run another.

The values a Linux interrupt handler returns: `IRQ_HANDLED` (this device raised it and it was dealt with), `IRQ_NONE` (not my device) and `IRQ_WAKE_THREAD` (wake the threaded handler). The kernel uses them to detect stuck shared lines.
One interrupt line used by several devices. Registered with `IRQF_SHARED`, every handler on the line is called and each must check its own device and return `IRQ_NONE` if it was not the source.

Notification that continues while a condition holds. A level-triggered interrupt line stays asserted until the device is serviced; level-triggered epoll keeps reporting a descriptor while it remains ready (the default, like select and poll).

A lock whose conventional non-RT implementation waits by spinning. Linux raw_spinlock_t remains a spinning lock; PREEMPT_RT changes spinlock_t into a sleeping-lock implementation, so the lock type and execution context determine permitted use.

Linux kernel allocation flags: GFP_KERNEL permits reclaim that may sleep and requires a sleepable context. GFP_ATOMIC is non-sleeping and can access reserves, but allocation may still fail; callers must handle that failure.

Virtual Function I/O: a Linux framework that safely gives a user-space process or VM direct access to a device, using the IOMMU for isolation. DPDK and VM passthrough bind NICs to the `vfio-pci` driver.
The kernel cache of file contents in RAM. A cache hit can avoid storage I/O; a miss may need storage work and block, although holes, end of file and other paths need not perform a device read.
A pair of rings used by NVMe and io_uring: the requester writes commands into a submission queue, and the other side writes results into a completion queue. In io_uring they are called the SQ and CQ.
To read and consume completion entries from a completion queue, advancing its head so the slots can be reused.
A scheduling problem where a high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task, which itself is starved by medium-priority work.
Repeatedly evicting and reloading the same cache lines because the working set does not fit, so most accesses miss and performance collapses.
One second of one CPU core's time. A task using one CPU-second per second keeps a whole core busy.
One tick of a CPU clock. At 3 GHz there are three billion ticks per second; instruction throughput and memory-access latency depend on architecture, memory state and workload.
The unit of frequency: one cycle per second. 1 GHz (gigahertz) is 10^9 Hz; CPU clocks run at a few GHz.

One billionth of a second. In the stated back-to-back, minimum untagged Ethernet occupancy model, a 10 Gbit/s link has 67.2 nanoseconds per frame; actual arrival spacing depends on traffic and link rules.
One millionth of a second. I/O latency is often measured in microseconds, but the unit alone implies no device performance.
One thousandth of a second (10^−3 s). A spinning disk seek takes a few milliseconds.
The basic unit of memory and storage: 8 bits, enough for one value from 0 to 255.
A binary digit, 0 or 1: the smallest unit of data. Network link speeds are quoted in bits per second.
Kibibyte: 1,024 bytes (2^10). Distinct from the kilobyte (kB), which is 1,000 bytes.
Mebibyte: 1,048,576 bytes (2^20 = 1,024 KiB).
Megabyte: 10^6 (one million) bytes; MB/s is megabytes per second. A gigabyte (GB) is 10^9 bytes. Not quite the same as a mebibyte (MiB).
Universal Serial Bus: a standard connecting peripherals such as keyboards and storage devices. A driver may wait for completion in a suitable sleepable context; hard IRQ context cannot sleep.
Disk space the kernel uses to hold memory pages evicted from RAM. Kernel `kmalloc` memory is never swapped out.

W. Richard Stevens' classification of how a process can perform input: blocking, non-blocking, I/O multiplexing, signal-driven and asynchronous I/O. They differ in how the process experiences waiting for data and copying it.
The classic book on Unix sockets by W. Richard Stevens, which introduced the five-I/O-models classification used in this module.

A socket mode in which a read may put the calling thread to sleep until data, end of stream or an error is available. Data already available may return immediately, and a successful read can be shorter than requested.

A socket mode in which an operation that would have to wait for readiness instead reports a condition such as EAGAIN. On Linux O_NONBLOCK is an open-file-description status flag shared by duplicated descriptors; supported operations and descriptor types matter.
Waiting on many descriptors in one call (`select`, `poll`, epoll, kqueue) that returns when any is ready, then performing the I/O on the ready ones. It lets one thread serve thousands of connections.

Asking the kernel to send a signal (normally `SIGIO`) when a descriptor becomes ready, enabled with `O_ASYNC` and `F_SETOWN` via `fcntl`. Signals can coalesce, so the program must re-check descriptor state.

I/O in which the program submits a request with a buffer, carries on, and later collects a completion saying the whole operation (including the copy) has finished. Examples: POSIX AIO, Windows IOCP, io_uring.

In POSIX terms, an I/O operation that blocks the requesting process until it completes. By that definition blocking, non-blocking, multiplexed and signal-driven reads are all synchronous, because the copy happens inside the caller's read.
An endpoint for network (or local) communication, represented in Unix by a file descriptor. Programs read and write sockets with `recv`/`send` or `read`/`write`.
A socket that carries a reliable, ordered byte stream with no message boundaries, normally TCP. A read may return fewer bytes than asked for.
A server socket bound to a port that accepts new connections. Each `accept()` on it returns a new connected socket.
The kernel queue of fully established connections waiting for the server to call `accept()` on a listening socket.

Kernel memory accounting and queued data associated with a socket. Receive queues hold unread input; send queues hold accepted output until protocol/ownership rules permit release. TCP acknowledgements and datagram transmission have different lifetimes; options such as SO_SNDBUF control limits.
Memory and code belonging to ordinary processes, as opposed to the kernel. Data moving between them must be copied or mapped across the boundary.
The memory and privileged code of the operating-system kernel, protected from user processes.

read reads from a descriptor; recv reads from a socket with additional flags. They return a byte count of signed type ssize_t or −1 on error. For a positive-length stream read, zero indicates EOF; zero-length requests and zero-size datagrams need separate interpretation.

write and send can accept fewer bytes than requested; retain and retry the unsent suffix as appropriate. Python socket.sendall instead attempts the whole payload and returns None on success; on failure it raises without reporting a usable partial count.
A read or write that transfers fewer bytes than requested. It is normal for sockets and pipes, so correct code loops or keeps the unsent remainder.

End of file. On a positive-length stream read, zero indicates receive EOF after preceding data is drained; the peer may have closed only its sending direction. Zero-length read requests and zero-size datagrams do not by themselves establish EOF.
TCP control flags: FIN means the sender has finished sending (a graceful close, seen by the reader as EOF); RST aborts the connection immediately (seen as a connection-reset error).
Closing only one direction of a TCP connection, usually with `shutdown()`: the peer reads EOF but can still send data the other way.

The usual SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that establishes a TCP connection. TCP can carry data in handshake segments under supported rules, so establishment is not universally completed before any data is sent.

The C variable (thread-local) where a failed system call stores a positive error number such as 2 (`ENOENT`). io_uring instead returns the error negated in the completion's `res` field. `strerror` turns a number into text.

The error a non-blocking call returns when it would otherwise have to wait (no data to read, no room to write). `EWOULDBLOCK` is the same condition and is equal to `EAGAIN` on Linux; Python raises `BlockingIOError`.

An error indicating interruption by a signal for an operation that reports it. Whether and how to retry depends on the call: preserve timeout/progress semantics, and do not blindly retry Linux close after EINTR.

Standard Unix error names: EPERM operation not permitted, ENOENT no such file, ENOSPC no space, EIO I/O error, EFAULT bad address, ENOBUFS no buffer space, EBUSY resource busy, EMFILE too many open files, EINVAL invalid argument, EINPROGRESS operation still in progress.
A small non-negative integer a process uses to refer to an open file, socket, pipe or other kernel object. Each process has a descriptor table mapping these numbers to open file descriptions.
example: A new process normally has descriptors 0, 1 and 2 open; the first socket it creates is usually 3.

definition: The kernel object behind one or more file descriptors, holding the file offset and status flags. `dup()` and `fork()` create new descriptors pointing to the same description; epoll registrations are tied to it.
A system call that creates a new file descriptor referring to the same open file description as an existing one.

The Unix call that creates a child with its own process state and descriptors referring to the parent’s open file descriptions. Linux uses copy-on-write for suitable private mappings, but page-table duplication and other work still have a cost.

Sharing suitable memory pages until a write requires a private copy. Linux fork uses this for private mappings, reducing eager copying without eliminating fork’s page-table, allocation and bookkeeping costs.
A server design that gives each client connection its own thread (or process) doing blocking I/O. Easy to write, but each thread costs a stack and scheduler work.
A long-established web server. Its prefork model uses one process per connection and its worker model one thread per connection, the classic blocking designs.

Memory for a thread’s call frames and local variables. Under Linux NPTL, a finite startup RLIMIT_STACK sets the default stack size; an unlimited limit uses an architecture-specific default. Attributes can override it. Virtual reservation, resident pages and guard size are distinct.
The part of a process's virtual memory that is actually held in RAM right now. Reserved but untouched pages are not resident.

The range of virtual addresses available to a process. A reservation is distinct from resident RAM; demand allocation, existing shared mappings, page faults and mapping flags determine when physical memory is associated with it.
The Linux kernel's per-thread record (`struct task_struct`) holding scheduling state, credentials, open files and more.

An open-file-description status flag requesting non-blocking behavior for supported operations. Linux ignores it for ordinary regular-file and block-device I/O, so storage waits can still occur; this does not mean every read necessarily accesses storage.
The system call for reading and changing a descriptor's flags, for example `F_GETFL` then `F_SETFL` with `O_NONBLOCK` added.
An ordinary data file on a file system, as opposed to a socket, pipe or device. Readiness APIs cannot report when a read of one will avoid the disk.
I/O where the kernel tells you when an operation can be done without blocking (a socket is readable) and you then perform it yourself. select, poll, epoll and kqueue work this way.

An interface that separates submitting an operation from collecting its completed result. Implementations may use kernel machinery or helper threads, and completion can occur before or after submission returns.

The bitmap type `select()` uses for each set of descriptors to watch, one bit per descriptor number (`FD_SET`, `FD_ZERO` and `FD_ISSET` set, clear and test bits). It holds `FD_SETSIZE` bits, 1024 on Linux glibc, and select overwrites it with the ready set on return.

The capacity of an fd_set bitmap, 1024 descriptor bits in Linux glibc. Using an out-of-range descriptor with FD_SET has undefined behavior; exact failure, including a fortify abort or memory overwrite, depends on implementation and build.

A multiplexing system call (System V, mid-1980s) that takes an array of `struct pollfd` entries (descriptor, requested events, returned `revents`). It has no 1024 limit but still checks every entry on every call.
One epoll object, created by `epoll_create1` and referred to by its own file descriptor. It holds the interest list (a red-black tree) and the ready list, and keeps them in the kernel between calls.

The epoll system calls: `epoll_create1` makes an instance, `epoll_ctl` adds, modifies or deletes a watched descriptor (`EPOLL_CTL_ADD`/`MOD`/`DEL`), and `epoll_wait` sleeps until events are ready and returns them.

epoll event bits: `EPOLLIN` means the descriptor is readable (or has a pending connection), `EPOLLOUT` means it is writable (send buffer has space). Watching EPOLLOUT permanently on a level-triggered socket makes the loop spin.

Notification driven by changes in readiness rather than by its continued presence. With epoll's `EPOLLET` you must read or write until `EAGAIN`, because unread data does not guarantee another notification.

An epoll flag that disables a watched registration after reporting an event until EPOLL_CTL_MOD rearms it. It supports a connection-ownership protocol; correct rearming and coordination of other access paths are still necessary.
An epoll flag (Linux 4.5) for descriptors watched by several epoll instances: an event wakes one or more of the exclusive waiters rather than all of them, reducing the thundering herd.
The set of descriptors (and events) an epoll instance watches, kept in the kernel between calls in a red-black tree.
The epoll instance's linked list of descriptors that have events pending, filled by wait-queue callbacks and drained by `epoll_wait`.
The `epoll_wait` argument giving the most events one call may return. Further ready descriptors are reported by later calls.
A self-balancing binary search tree whose height stays at most about 2 × log₂(n), so search, insert and delete take O(log n). epoll uses one for its interest list and nginx for its timers.
An array of bits, one per item, where bit k says whether item k is in the set. `fd_set` is a bitmap indexed by descriptor number.

A Linux mechanism for tasks or callbacks waiting for an object’s state to change. Wakeup rules, including exclusive waiters, determine which entries are notified; epoll attaches callbacks to relevant wait queues.
A function you hand to a library or the kernel so it can be called later when something happens, such as data arriving on a socket.
In C, an operation the standard places no requirements on, such as writing past the end of an array. Anything may happen, from silent memory corruption to a crash.
An access that writes outside a buffer’s valid range. In C this can cause undefined behavior; memory corruption is possible but not guaranteed. Out-of-range unchecked FD_SET use is one example.
A glibc and compiler hardening option that adds runtime checks to some library calls, such as catching an out-of-range `FD_SET`, and aborts instead of corrupting memory.
A notification that is no longer true by the time you act on it, for example readiness for a socket another thread has drained or a connection already closed earlier in the same batch.

Waking many waiting threads or processes for one event that only one of them can handle, so the rest wake for nothing (for example, all workers woken for one new connection, then all but one getting `EAGAIN` from `accept`).

A socket option (Linux 3.9) letting several sockets bind the same port, each with its own accept queue; the kernel spreads new connections across them. `SO_REUSEADDR` is a different option that permits re-binding an address quickly after restart.

The event-notification interface of FreeBSD (2000), macOS, NetBSD and OpenBSD. One `kevent` call can apply a list of changes and return ready events, and filters cover sockets, files, processes, signals and timers.
The kind of event a kqueue registration watches: `EVFILT_READ`/`EVFILT_WRITE` for descriptors, `EVFILT_VNODE` for file changes, `EVFILT_PROC` for process events, `EVFILT_SIGNAL` and `EVFILT_TIMER`.

kqueue flags: `EV_ADD` registers, `EV_CLEAR` resets state after delivery (edge-like), `EV_ONESHOT` deletes after one delivery, `EV_DISPATCH` disables until re-enabled. The changelist and eventlist are the two arrays passed to `kevent`.
Linux interfaces that turn other events into file descriptors so epoll can watch them: `signalfd` for signals, `timerfd` for timers, `pidfd` for a process and `inotify` for file-system changes.
The 1983 release of the Berkeley Software Distribution of Unix, which introduced the sockets API and `select`. Its descendants FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD share kqueue.
Apple's desktop operating system, built on a BSD-derived Unix core, so it offers kqueue rather than epoll.
AT&T's commercial Unix line of the 1980s, which introduced `poll`.
Solaris and illumos's event-notification interface, comparable to epoll and kqueue. Redis's ae library can use it (evport).
Dan Kegel's 1999 question of how one server can handle ten thousand simultaneous clients, which drove the move from select/poll to epoll and kqueue. C10M is the later goal of ten million.
Linux kernel releases are numbered major.minor (for example 5.1 in 2019, 6.6 in 2023). Features in this module, such as io_uring or EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, exist only from a particular version onward.
`SIGIO` is the signal sent for signal-driven I/O. With `F_SETSIG` and `SA_SIGINFO`, Linux can instead send a queued real-time signal carrying the descriptor and event.
The rule that a signal handler may only call functions that are safe to run while interrupting arbitrary code (async-signal-safe), such as `write`, but not `printf` or `malloc`.

Notifications delivered to a process or thread. SIGHUP denotes a terminal/controlling-process hangup by default and is conventionally repurposed by nginx for reload; SIGSEGV reports an invalid memory reference.
The IEEE standard defining the Unix system interface (system calls, C library functions, shell), so programs can be portable between Unix-like systems.
The POSIX asynchronous I/O interface: `aio_read` submits a read described by a `struct aiocb`, and `aio_error`/`aio_return` collect the result. glibc implements it with user-space helper threads.
The GNU C Library, the standard C library on most Linux distributions, providing wrappers for system calls and functions such as POSIX AIO.
Linux's older kernel asynchronous I/O interface (`io_submit`), mostly useful with `O_DIRECT` files and with operations and paths that can still block.

An open flag requesting a direct-I/O path that normally avoids the page cache. Alignment and support requirements depend on kernel/filesystem; unsupported or misaligned cases may fail or fall back to buffered I/O. The flag alone does not make I/O asynchronous.
I/O completion ports: Windows' completion-based I/O interface. You issue overlapped operations with buffers, and finished operations appear as completion packets on the port.
An event-loop design that waits for readiness and dispatches each ready descriptor to a handler, which then performs the I/O. Built on select, epoll or kqueue.

An event-loop design where operations are started asynchronously and the loop dispatches completion handlers when they finish. Built on IOCP or io_uring; Python's `ProactorEventLoop` uses IOCP on Windows.

Language syntax allowing an asynchronous function to suspend while awaiting a result. Awaiting an already-complete result need not yield, and syntax alone does not specify an event loop or underlying I/O mechanism.
A function that can suspend itself and be resumed later, keeping its local state. Python's `async def` functions are coroutines run by the asyncio event loop.
Python's standard library for writing single-threaded concurrent code with `async`/`await`, built on an event loop (selector-based on Unix by default).
Python's standard wrapper over epoll, kqueue, poll or select. `DefaultSelector` picks the best one for the platform, and `EVENT_READ`/`EVENT_WRITE` say which readiness to watch.

asyncio's built-in pool of threads used to run blocking functions without stalling the event loop, for example via `loop.run_in_executor(None, ...)`. asyncio also uses it for some built-in blocking work such as name resolution.

Socket flags: MSG_WAITALL requests waiting for the requested receive length, but errors, signals or disconnects can still cause a short return. MSG_PEEK observes without consuming; supported MSG_ZEROCOPY sends have separate completion and buffer-lifetime rules.
Optional periodic probes TCP sends on an idle connection to check the peer is still there. Successful probes carry no application data.

The standard C library function that turns a host name into addresses, using `/etc/hosts`, DNS and other configured sources. It blocks, so Node's `dns.lookup` runs it on the libuv thread pool; `dns.resolve` queries DNS directly instead.

Linux's completion-based I/O interface (Linux 5.1, 2019, by Jens Axboe). The application writes requests into a shared submission ring and reads results from a shared completion ring, so many operations can be submitted and reaped with few or no system calls.
A fixed-size array used as a queue whose positions wrap round to the start, tracked by a head (where the consumer reads) and a tail (where the producer writes).

io_uring's two rings: the submission queue (SQ), where the application places requests, and the completion queue (CQ), where the kernel places results. By default the CQ has twice as many entries as the SQ.
Submission queue entry: one io_uring request (normally 64 bytes) giving the opcode, target descriptor, buffer address and length, file offset and a `user_data` tag.
Completion queue entry: one io_uring result (normally 16 bytes) holding the request's `user_data`, a `res` value (bytes transferred, a new descriptor, or a negative errno) and flags.
The two counters of a ring buffer. The producer writes entries at the tail and advances it; the consumer reads at the head and advances it. Each counter is written by only one side.
A pattern where one party adds items to a shared queue and another removes them. With exactly one producer and one consumer, a ring needs only careful memory ordering rather than a lock.

Rules about the order in which one CPU's memory writes become visible to other CPUs (or the kernel). Lock-free rings use acquire and release operations so an entry is fully written before the index that publishes it.

A progress property of a concurrent algorithm: the system as a whole continues completing operations despite individual threads being delayed. It does not guarantee each thread completes promptly, and absence of an explicit mutex alone does not prove the property.
The system call that maps a file or kernel object into a process's address space. io_uring's rings are mmapped so the application and kernel share the same memory.

A number obtainable by multiplying 2 by itself a whole number of times, including 1, 2, 64 and 256. The io_uring ring capacities discussed here are powers of two, so their slot calculation can use a bit mask; circular buffers in general need not have such a capacity.
An operation (written `&`) that compares two numbers bit by bit and keeps a 1 only where both have a 1. `i & (E − 1)` keeps the low bits of i, which equals i mod E when E is a power of two.
Operation code: the field in an SQE saying which operation to perform, such as READ, WRITE, ACCEPT or SEND.
A 64-bit value the application puts in each SQE, which the kernel copies unchanged into the matching CQE. Usually a pointer to the request's state, it is how completions are matched to requests.
Completions arriving in a different order from submission, for example a cached read finishing before an earlier read that went to disk.

io_uring's three system calls: `io_uring_setup` creates a ring, `io_uring_enter` submits new SQEs and optionally waits for completions, and `io_uring_register` registers long-lived files, buffers and restrictions.
The helper library most programs use for io_uring. It wraps the raw syscalls and ring memory-ordering rules in functions such as `io_uring_get_sqe`, `io_uring_submit` and `io_uring_wait_cqe`.
Application binary interface: the exact binary layout and calling rules (structure sizes, field offsets, register use) a program must follow to talk to the kernel or a library.

An io_uring mode in which a kernel thread polls the submission queue, so the application can submit with no system call. After `sq_thread_idle` milliseconds without work the thread sleeps and sets `IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP`, and the application must wake it with `io_uring_enter`.
An io_uring mode that polls the device for I/O completions instead of waiting for interrupts, for supported direct-I/O devices. Distinct from SQPOLL, which polls the submission queue.

Files registered with an io_uring instance and referred to by a registered index. This avoids ordinary per-operation descriptor-table lookup while retaining resource registration, lifetime and internal bookkeeping.
Buffers registered with an io_uring ring so their pages are pinned and mapped once, then reused by `READ_FIXED` and `WRITE_FIXED` operations.
io_uring's internal pool of kernel worker threads, used for operations that cannot be done inline or by polling, such as a buffered read that misses the page cache on some file systems.

Performing an io_uring operation in the submitting context rather than first handing it to a worker. Whether an operation attempts this, arms polling or uses io-wq depends on opcode, flags and kernel implementation.

Supported io_uring operations where one request can produce multiple completions, such as accept since Linux 5.19 and receive since 6.0. Check IORING_CQE_F_MORE on every CQE; absence means the request ended, including normal termination and conditions such as buffer exhaustion.
An io_uring feature where the application supplies a pool of buffers and the kernel picks one only when data actually arrives, so idle connections need not each hold a dedicated buffer.

SQEs joined by IOSQE_IO_LINK execute in dependency order. Documented failures can cancel later soft-linked requests; linking does not automatically set a later write length from an earlier read result.

Sending data while avoiding a particular ordinary payload copy. Supported io_uring zero-copy sends can require a later notification CQE before buffer reuse; copying fallbacks and completion flags matter. sendfile moves file data to another descriptor without passing it through an application buffer.
A CQE flag meaning more completions will follow for the same request, for example a later notification that a zero-copy send's buffer is free, or further results from a multishot operation.

The interval during which an I/O buffer must remain valid and must not be reused incompatibly. The operation’s documented ownership rules determine release: a normal completion, multishot use or a zero-copy-send notification can differ.
When the completion queue is full and more completions arrive. With `IORING_FEAT_NODROP` the kernel normally parks extra CQEs in an internal backlog until there is room, at a memory and speed cost.
The io_uring operation that requests cancellation of a pending request, identified by its `user_data`. Cancellation is asynchronous: the original may still complete.

An io_uring feature describing when request metadata referenced by an SQE may be released. Follow opcode and submission-mode rules, especially SQPOLL consumption; payload buffers generally remain valid through operation completion.
io_uring registration that limits which opcodes and flags a ring may use. It must be applied while the ring is created disabled (`IORING_SETUP_R_DISABLED`) and before it is enabled.
A Linux sysctl (6.6): 0 allows everyone to create io_uring rings, 1 only privileged processes or members of `kernel.io_uring_group`, 2 nobody. Existing rings keep working.
A Linux interface for reading and setting kernel parameters at run time, such as `net.core.netdev_budget` or `kernel.io_uring_disabled`.

Secure computing mode: a Linux mechanism for restricting system calls. Container policy depends on runtime, version and configuration: Docker ordinarily supplies a default profile on supported setups, whereas a Kubernetes workload with no profile specified can run Unconfined when seccompDefault is disabled. Inspect effective workload and node settings rather than assuming RuntimeDefault.
A list of things that are explicitly permitted, with everything else denied.
Moby is the open-source project behind Docker Engine. Its default seccomp profile is an allowlist that, in the versions inspected, omits the io_uring syscalls.
Google's Kubernetes-based capture-the-flag programme and vulnerability reward programme (VRP), which pays researchers for working Linux kernel exploits.
Google's operating systems for Chromebooks (ChromeOS) and phones (Android), both built on the Linux kernel.

Security or tracing tools that watch system calls as they are entered. They do not automatically see each io_uring operation, because many operations go through the rings rather than separate syscalls.
A Linux file descriptor holding a counter that one thread can increment to wake another waiting on it, often used to wake an event loop or signal io_uring completions.
The system call that opens a file relative to a directory descriptor; io_uring can perform it as an operation.
An I/O scheduling priority attached to a request; io_uring SQEs have an `ioprio` field for it.
Input/output operations per second: a measure of how many separate reads or writes a storage system completes each second.
The number of I/O requests outstanding at once. Fast SSDs need many in flight to reach their full throughput.

Families of speculative-execution side-channel vulnerabilities disclosed in 2018. Mitigations can add overhead on affected systems, with costs depending on CPU, mitigation choice, kernel and workload; no universal syscall-cost increase is implied.
A PostgreSQL 18 setting choosing how the server performs asynchronous I/O; `io_uring` is one option when built with support.
A single thread that repeatedly waits for I/O readiness or the next timer, then runs the callbacks for whatever happened. It lets one thread serve many connections, as long as no callback blocks.
A design where the program reacts to events (data arrived, timer fired, connection closed) delivered by an event loop rather than dedicating a blocked thread to each task.
The step of an event loop that maps each reported event to the handler registered for it and calls it.
A loop runs an ordinary callback until it returns before dispatching the next one on that loop. Exclusively owned state often needs no inter-thread lock, but re-entry and shared data require care.
Code that can be safely entered again before an earlier call has finished, for example a callback that triggers another callback on the same loop.
Running something slow (a synchronous file read, heavy computation, a sleep) on the event-loop thread, which freezes every connection that loop serves.

Delay between a timer’s intended scheduling threshold and when its callback actually runs. It can reveal blocking or overloaded loops, but OS scheduling, runtime pauses and timer resolution also affect it.
Deeply nested callbacks that make control flow and error handling hard to follow; async/await was introduced largely to fix it.
A buffer threshold: above the high-water mark a producer is paused (backpressure), and below the low-water mark it resumes. Node streams use `highWaterMark`.

A priority-queue structure in which each parent’s key is no greater than its children’s, so the root has a minimum key. For a binary min-heap with n items, insertion and removing the minimum take O(log n), and inspecting the root takes O(1).
The smallest time step a clock or timer can resolve. A wait cannot end more precisely than this, so a requested 1 ms timeout may fire later.
The C library that provides Node.js's event loop, thread pool and cross-platform I/O (epoll, kqueue, IOCP, optionally io_uring).
The fixed stages of each libuv loop iteration: pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll (wait and run I/O callbacks), check (setImmediate), close callbacks and timers.

A JavaScript runtime built on V8 and libuv. Each event loop executes its callbacks on its owning thread; worker_threads can run additional JavaScript threads. Some asynchronous file, name-resolution, crypto and compression work uses libuv workers.

Node.js functions scheduling callbacks: setTimeout requests a timer threshold, while setImmediate schedules the check phase. Neither guarantees exact timing; phase and scheduling context determine when callbacks can run.

Node.js nextTick callbacks and promise microtasks are serviced outside the ordinary event-loop phases. nextTick precedes promise microtasks in typical CommonJS callback contexts, while ES-module evaluation can differ; endlessly refilling either queue can starve I/O.
Node.js's two module systems: CommonJS (`require`, `__filename`) and ES modules (`import`). ES-module evaluation is itself driven by microtasks, which can change callback order.
A collection of worker threads that take queued jobs, avoiding one new thread per job. Some pools have a configured fixed size (such as libuv’s), while other implementations resize dynamically.
The environment variable setting libuv's thread-pool size: 4 by default, up to 1,024.
Password-hashing functions deliberately designed to be slow (PBKDF2 and scrypt). Node runs their asynchronous versions on the libuv thread pool.
A widely used compression library (deflate/gzip). Node runs asynchronous zlib work on the libuv thread pool.
Network File System: a protocol for accessing files on a remote server as if they were local. Reads can be slow, which ties up thread-pool workers.
A widely used web server and reverse proxy built on one event loop per worker process.

nginx's process model: a master process reads configuration and binds ports, and worker processes (count set by `worker_processes`) each run an event loop handling up to `worker_connections` connections.
An nginx directive (1.7.11) that sends file reads which may block to a thread pool, so a page-cache miss does not stall a worker's event loop.

Starting workers with new configuration while old workers finish existing connections. This supports service continuity, but configuration errors, shutdown deadlines and failed connections mean zero loss is not an unconditional guarantee.

CPU affinity limits where tasks or interrupts may execute. Aligning queue interrupts and consuming workers can improve cache locality, but hardware and software flow steering are separate mappings and do not automatically align.
Linux control groups: a kernel feature that groups processes and limits their CPU, memory and I/O. Containers use them, so a process may see fewer usable CPUs than the machine has.
Several threads trying to take the same lock at once, so some wait. It limits how well shared-state designs scale across cores.
Redis's own small event library, which wraps epoll, kqueue, event ports or select chosen at build time.

Redis commands: KEYS scans the keyspace, SCAN iterates with a cursor and COUNT hint, and SMEMBERS returns an entire set. DEL freeing depends on lazy-free configuration; UNLINK detaches keys and can defer expensive freeing. GET reads a string value.
A small scripting language Redis can run inside the server; a script executes atomically on the main thread, so a slow one blocks every client.
Redis's option to reclaim memory of deleted keys in a background thread instead of on the main thread.
Redis Database file: a point-in-time snapshot of the dataset written by a forked child process.
Sending several Redis commands without waiting for each reply, so network round trips are shared; the server still executes each command.

Redis 6.0 introduced configurable socket I/O threads while ordinary commands remained serial on the main thread. In that release, threaded reads additionally require io-threads-do-reads yes; inspect the deployed version rather than assuming identical later implementations.
Redis's sharded mode, where the keyspace is split across several independent instances, each with its own single command thread.
Node.js's module for running several worker processes, each with its own event loop, sharing one server port.
Event-loop-based network servers and libraries: Netty (Java framework), HAProxy (load balancer) and Envoy (proxy, one loop per worker thread).

A C++ framework organized around application shards and event loops, commonly one per core, that underlies ScyllaDB. Its shared-nothing application model reduces shared mutable data; it does not imply every runtime or OS component has no locks.

A design giving each application shard a core and ownership of its data, with cross-shard work expressed through messages. It reduces shared mutable application state; implementation details can still use shared memory and synchronization.
Communicating between threads or processes by sending messages rather than sharing memory protected by locks.

A regular-expression performance failure in which a backtracking matcher explores excessively many alternatives for certain inputs, potentially taking exponential time. Regular expressions in general do not all have this behavior.

Linux’s mechanism for selecting tasks to kill under qualifying out-of-memory conditions, including cgroup limits. Not every allocation failure invokes it, and the exact choice depends on policy and context.
asyncio's thread-safe way to schedule a callback on an event loop from another thread; it also wakes the loop.
A limit after which something inactive is shut down or put to sleep: an idle connection closed by a server, or io_uring's SQPOLL thread sleeping after `sq_thread_idle`.
The moment a timer is due to fire. An event loop keeps timers ordered by expiry and sleeps until the earliest one.
A network interface card (NIC) with its own programmable processors, able to run offloaded work such as XDP programs or packet filtering on the card itself.
A unit of data sent over a network, with headers saying where it is going. On Ethernet each packet travels inside a frame.

The link-layer unit transmitted by Ethernet. An untagged Ethernet II frame has a 14-byte header, payload/padding and 4-byte FCS, with a minimum 64-byte frame. The lesson’s rate model adds 8 preamble/SFD byte-times and a 12-byte-time gap; tagging and physical-link rules need their own accounting.
Frame check sequence: the 4-byte checksum (a CRC) at the end of an Ethernet frame, used to detect corruption.
The 7-byte preamble and 1-byte start frame delimiter sent before every Ethernet frame so the receiver can synchronise; together 8 bytes of wire time.

The idle interval between Ethernet frames, commonly modeled as 12 byte-times (96 bit-times). Physical-interface rules and receive-side tolerances can differ; the worked minimum-frame rate uses the stated 12-byte-time assumption.
The time a link takes to transmit one bit (or one byte) at its rate. At 10 Gbit/s one bit-time is 0.1 ns.
The unit of link speed: how many bits a link carries each second (bit/s). 1 Mbit/s is 10^6 bit/s and 1 Gbit/s (also written Gb/s) is 10^9 bit/s, so a 10 Gbit/s link carries 10^10 bits each second.
How many packets a link or system handles each second. Small packets mean a high packet rate and less time per packet.
Dynamic random-access memory, commonly used as a computer’s main memory. Access latency depends on hardware, cache state, locality, contention and overlap; no fixed latency is implied.
The Linux kernel's packet structure ("socket buffer"): metadata plus pointers to the packet's headers and data, passed between the network layers.

Linux’s event-processing abstraction for network drivers. Conventional operation schedules budgeted receive polling after an interrupt, but busy polling, threaded modes and queue mappings vary by configuration.

Receive-work limits: a NAPI instance’s poll receives a budget, commonly related to its configured weight, while a conventional receive-softirq round also has overall packet/time limits through netdev_budget and netdev_budget_usecs. TX completions follow different budget rules.

A per-CPU softnet counter incremented when a receive-processing budget or time condition triggers. It is a signal to correlate with load and drops, rather than proof of an exact remaining backlog or CPU-capacity limit.
A Linux file with one row per CPU of hexadecimal network-receive counters: packets processed, packets dropped, time squeezes and more.
A Linux file showing, per CPU, how many times each softirq type has run.
Base-16 notation using digits 0–9 and a–f; 0x8100 is 33,024 in decimal.

Generic Receive Offload combines eligible packets of a flow into larger skbs so later stack layers process fewer units. Protocol, kernel, driver and packet-layout restrictions determine what can merge.

TCP segmentation offload lets the stack hand a supporting NIC a larger TCP aggregate for hardware splitting into segments. Generic Segmentation Offload performs supported splitting in software before driver transmission; sizes and features depend on the device and kernel.
The kernel function through which drivers pass received skbs into the core networking stack.
The Linux packet-filtering framework; iptables and its successor nftables are the tools that configure its firewall and NAT rules.
The five fields that identify a connection or flow: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port and protocol.
A sequence of packets sharing the same 5-tuple, for example all packets of one TCP connection.

A large, long-lived network flow, for example a backup transfer. Under stable conventional Receive Side Scaling it generally maps to one RX queue, while IRQ affinity and software steering determine later CPU placement.
TCP acknowledgement: a segment telling the sender which bytes (by sequence number) have arrived.

Receive Side Scaling: a NIC hashes supported packet fields and maps the hash through an indirection table to an RX queue. Stable per-flow mapping helps preserve order; interrupt affinity and software steering separately determine later CPU placement.
The hash function commonly used by NICs for Receive Side Scaling, computed over the flow's addresses and ports with a configurable (often random) key.
The table a NIC uses for Receive Side Scaling: the low bits of a packet's hash index it, and each entry names an RX queue.
One of a NIC's independent receive (RX) or transmit (TX) queues, each with its own ring and usually its own interrupt, so different CPUs can handle them.
The Linux command for viewing and setting NIC options, such as the number of queues (`ethtool -L`) and the Receive Side Scaling table (`ethtool -x`).
Receive Packet Steering: Receive Side Scaling done in software. The kernel hashes a packet in softirq and queues it on another CPU's backlog, for NICs with too few queues.
Receive Flow Steering: steers each flow to the CPU where the application thread reading it last ran, so its data is hot in that core's cache. Accelerated RFS asks the NIC to do the steering.
Transmit Packet Steering: chooses a TX queue from the sending CPU (or receive queue), reducing contention on shared transmit queues.
A per-CPU kernel queue where RPS places packets for that CPU to process in its own softirq.
A Linux daemon that periodically moves interrupts between CPUs to spread load; it can undo manual IRQ affinity settings.

Non-uniform memory access: memory-access cost depends on where processors and memory reside in the hardware topology. Nodes can exist within one socket as well as across sockets; placement of data, threads and devices can affect locality.
Limits on how much unacknowledged data TCP may send: the receive window is what the receiver has room for; the congestion window is the sender's estimate of what the network can carry.
TCP algorithms (such as CUBIC or BBR) that adjust the sending rate to avoid overloading the network.
The Linux traffic-control (tc) component that queues and schedules outgoing packets on an interface, for example `fq` (fair queueing with pacing) or `fq_codel` (fair queueing with delay control).

A device/driver indication that transmit resources can be reclaimed under its ownership protocol. This can be distinct from final wire transmission and does not prove remote receipt or application processing.
The layers of kernel code that process packets between the NIC driver and sockets: link layer, IP, TCP/UDP and socket queues.
Data Plane Development Kit: libraries and poll-mode drivers that let a user-space process drive a NIC directly, bypassing the kernel network stack for very high packet rates.
Storage Performance Development Kit: the storage counterpart of DPDK, with user-space polled NVMe drivers.

Moving part of a device data path outside the ordinary kernel network or storage stack, for example with DPDK or SPDK. Kernel setup/control, copies and synchronization can remain; AF_XDP has supported copy and zero-copy modes.
The part of a network system that forwards or processes the actual packets, as opposed to the control plane that configures it.

A DPDK driver interface commonly polled from userspace to receive/transmit packet bursts. Dedicated busy-poll use avoids waiting for a packet interrupt; supported interrupt/power-management modes and hardware/software PMDs vary.

Pages larger than the architecture’s base page size, for example 2 MiB or 1 GiB on supporting x86 systems. Larger mappings can cover more memory per TLB entry; supported sizes and actual performance depend on platform and workload.
An address translation not found in the TLB, so the CPU must walk the page tables, costing extra memory accesses.
A NIC driver model where the kernel keeps the device while selected traffic is steered to a user-space (DPDK) application, so both can share one NIC.

Linux networking tools: tcpdump captures traffic visible at supported capture points, while ss inspects sockets. An exclusive DPDK data path bypasses ordinary kernel-stack visibility; capture and integration mechanisms vary.
A TCP/IP implementation running inside an application rather than the kernel, needed with kernel-bypass designs; F-Stack is one built on DPDK.

A facility for loading programs checked by a verifier and attaching them to supported hooks, including networking and tracing. Verification enforces documented safety rules but is not proof that kernel, JIT or program logic has no bugs.
The kernel component that checks every eBPF program before loading: it must terminate, use valid types and only access memory it can prove is in bounds.
Kernel data structures (hash tables, arrays, ring buffers and more) shared between eBPF programs and user space.
A fixed instrumentation point in the kernel where tracing tools or eBPF programs can attach to observe events.
eXpress Data Path: an eBPF hook at the very start of a driver's receive path. Native XDP runs before an skb is allocated; generic XDP runs later with broader support; offloaded XDP runs on the NIC.

XDP return actions include DROP, PASS, TX, REDIRECT and ABORTED. They respectively discard, continue normally, transmit back through the interface, redirect through a supported target, or signal an aborted/drop path.

Linux sockets for passing selected XDP traffic between kernel networking and application-managed UMEM buffers. Driver and mode determine copy or zero-copy support and performance; other traffic can remain on the ordinary stack.
Splitting an IP packet too large for a link into fragments, reassembled at the destination. The MF ("more fragments") flag and fragment offset in the IPv4 header mark them.
Virtual LAN: a 4-byte tag (EtherType 0x8100) inserted in an Ethernet frame to place it on a logical network. Tagged frames shift the IP header and must be parsed specially.
The 2-byte field in an Ethernet header saying which protocol the payload carries; 0x0800 (`ETH_P_IP`) is IPv4.
Big-endian byte order used in packet headers. `htons`/`ntohs` (and their BPF versions) convert 16-bit values between host and network order.
A value calculated over selected data to help detect corruption. IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 has no corresponding base-header checksum. TCP and UDP have protocol-specific checksum rules.
A 16-bit number in a TCP or UDP header identifying which application on a host a packet is for.
A large CDN and network-security company that has published its use of XDP for dropping attack traffic.
Meta's open-source layer-4 load balancer built on XDP.
A load balancer that routes by transport-layer information (addresses and TCP/UDP ports) without looking at application data.
An eBPF-based networking, security and observability project for Kubernetes; it can replace kube-proxy, the default component that implements Kubernetes service routing (often with iptables).
An open-source system for running containers across a cluster of machines, scheduling them and wiring up their networking.

Understanding system behavior through outputs such as metrics, logs and traces. eBPF can instrument supported kernel/application events; overhead and completeness depend on the program, hook and workload.

The particular sequence of code a request or packet runs through, for example the receive path from the NIC driver up to a socket. Two ways of doing the same job (an interrupt path and a polling path) can have very different costs.
example: Native XDP drops a packet early in the driver's receive path, before the kernel allocates an skb.

definition: Splitting a TCP byte stream into segments small enough to fit the link's MTU, each with its own TCP/IP headers. With segmentation offload the kernel passes a large chunk down and the NIC (TCP segmentation offload) or the kernel just before the driver (GSO) does the split.

Temporarily preventing delivery of a device interrupt under a defined device/controller protocol. Masking does not itself prove events cannot be lost; the driver must coordinate acknowledgement, polling and unmasking to avoid races.
